title: Cauchy–Schwarz: The Dot Product Has a Ceiling
topic: The Cauchy–Schwarz inequality |⟨u,v⟩| ≤ ‖u‖·‖v‖ caps the dot product by the product of lengths. Sweeping the angle between u and v traces ⟨u,v⟩ between ±‖u‖·‖v‖, with equality exactly when u and v are parallel. The bound is what makes cos θ = ⟨u,v⟩/(‖u‖·‖v‖) a number in [−1, 1].

beats.narration: How big can the dot product of two vectors get?

elements.content: How big can u dot v get?

beats.narration: Fix the lengths of u and v. The lengths of u and v multiplied set a ceiling — the dot product can never exceed it in size.

elements.content: Two arrows u (amber, length 3) and v (teal, length 2) drawn from origin on a grid
the inequality holds for any two vectors — and the ceiling is the product of their lengths

beats.narration: Spin v around. The dot product rises and falls, but the trace stays bounded between plus and minus the ceiling — it kisses the bound exactly when v lines up with u.

elements.content: u fixed along +x, v rotates 0 to 2π; arc shows angle
Right panel chart: horizontal lines at +‖u‖·‖v‖ and −‖u‖·‖v‖; trace of u·v plotted as θ sweeps
live readout of θ, cos θ and u·v

beats.narration: Equality holds when u and v are parallel — same direction gives plus the ceiling, opposite directions give minus. Anything in between misses.

elements.content: Three small tiles: u and v parallel (= +max), antiparallel (= −max), generic (strict < max)
equality iff v is a scalar multiple of u

beats.narration: Cauchy and Schwarz: the dot product is squeezed by the lengths. That is what makes cosine of theta a real number between minus one and one.

elements.content: the bound that lets the angle exist
